questions.stem: What does the area between a velocity-time line and the time axis represent?

options.text: The distance travelled during that interval
options.explanation: Enclosed area multiplies velocity by time, which is exactly a distance.

options.text: The acceleration gained
options.explanation: Acceleration is the gradient of the line, not the area beneath it.

options.text: The average velocity
options.explanation: Average velocity would be a height, not an area; the area counts metres.

options.text: The time the journey lasted
options.explanation: Time is the base of the shape, already measured along the horizontal axis.

questions.stem: The region under a straight rising section is a triangle with base 8 s and height 12 m/s. What distance does it encode?

options.text: 48 m, from one half of 8 × 12
options.explanation: Triangle area = ½ × base × height = ½ × 8 × 12 = 48 m.

options.text: 96 m, from 8 × 12
options.explanation: 96 m is the full rectangle; the triangular half is wanted for a rising section.

options.text: 20 m, from 8 + 12
options.explanation: Areas multiply their sides; adding a time and a velocity has no meaning.
That quotient would be an acceleration, not the distance the area encodes.

questions.stem: A section of line sits perfectly flat at 9 m/s for 7 s. What shape is the enclosed region and what distance does it hold?

options.text: A rectangle holding 63 m, from 9 × 7
options.explanation: Constant velocity makes a rectangle: base 7 s times height 9 m/s = 63 m.

options.text: A triangle holding 31.5 m
options.explanation: Triangles belong to changing velocity; a flat section makes a rectangle.

options.text: A rectangle holding 16 m, from 9 + 7
options.explanation: The sides multiply; adding gives neither an area nor a distance.

options.text: No region exists under a flat line
options.explanation: A flat line above the axis encloses the largest rectangle of all: velocity times the whole interval.

questions.stem: Why does the area under this graph carry the unit metres rather than any other unit?

options.text: Because the sides multiply metres per second by seconds, and the seconds cancel
options.explanation: (m/s) × (s) leaves m: the unit arithmetic is the whole justification.

options.text: Because areas are always measured in metres
options.explanation: Area units follow the axes: on a distance-time graph the enclosed area would be m·s, not m.

options.text: Because the graph is drawn on squared paper
options.explanation: The paper is irrelevant; the unit comes from the quantities on the two axes.

options.text: Because velocity is defined as distance divided by area
options.explanation: Velocity is distance over time; the area rule follows from multiplying back by time.

questions.stem: An object decelerates in a straight line from 20 m/s to rest over 10 s. Which calculation gives the distance it covers while stopping?

options.explanation: A straight fall to rest is a triangle: base 10 s, height 20 m/s, area 100 m.
200 m is the full rectangle; stopping in a straight line fills only half of it.
That quotient is the deceleration in m/s², not a distance.

options.text: 0 m, because the object ends at rest
options.explanation: Ending at rest says nothing about the ground covered; the triangle holds 100 m.

questions.stem: State the two area formulas used to read distances from a velocity-time graph and say which motion each matches.
questions.modelAnswer: Triangle: area = ½ × base × height, for changing velocity (accelerating or decelerating). Rectangle: area = base × height, for constant velocity.

questions.stem: Recall what the height and the base of an enclosed region correspond to on the graph's axes.
questions.modelAnswer: The height is a velocity read from the vertical axis and the base is a time interval read from the horizontal axis.

questions.stem: Explain why a straight rising section encloses a triangle rather than a rectangle on a velocity-time graph.
questions.modelAnswer: A rising straight line starts low and ends high, so the region between it and the axis is a right triangle whose sloping top is the line itself. A rectangle would need the line to stay at one constant height, which is exactly the constant-velocity case instead.

questions.stem: A scooter holds 6.0 m/s for 12 s, then rises in a straight line from 6.0 m/s to 14 m/s over 8.0 s. Calculate the distance covered in each section.
questions.modelAnswer: Cruise: rectangle 6.0 × 12 = 72 m. Rise: triangle ½ × 8.0 × 14 = 56 m. The scooter covers 72 m then 56 m in the two sections.

questions.stem: A journey's velocity-time region divides into five enclosed sections. How is the total distance obtained?

options.text: Every area is calculated and the five results are added
options.explanation: Each area is a distance; the journey total is their sum.

options.text: Only the largest section's area matters
options.explanation: Every interval contributes its metres; dropping sections loses part of the journey.

options.text: The five areas are averaged
options.explanation: A mean of areas has no physical meaning; distances accumulate by addition.

options.text: The areas are multiplied together
options.explanation: Multiplying metre-counts together would give m⁵, not a distance.

questions.stem: In the worked car journey, one region needs splitting into a triangle and a rectangle. What does that split tell you about the motion in that interval?

options.text: The velocity changed part-way through the interval, first rising then holding
options.explanation: A triangle plus rectangle side by side is the signature of a rise that then flattens within one interval.

options.text: The car reversed direction during the interval
options.explanation: Reversal would appear below the axis, not as an internal split of an above-axis region.

options.text: The velocity stayed constant throughout
options.explanation: A single rectangle would cover that; the split exists because the profile bends.

options.text: The graph was drawn inaccurately
options.explanation: The split is the lawful reading of a two-part profile, not a drawing fault.

questions.stem: The worked journey's five areas are 350 m, 525 m, 75 m, 350 m and 875 m. Which arithmetic check confirms the total?

options.explanation: The five areas sum to 2175 m, the journey's total distance.
A product of five metre-values is dimensionally absurd for a distance.
Ratio-form combinations of areas are not part of the summation rule.
Subtracting component distances from the largest gives no journey quantity.

questions.stem: The distance travelled between 70 s and 90 s of the worked journey is wanted. Which reading is correct?

options.text: The areas standing on the 70-90 s slice of the base, which are areas 3 and 4
options.explanation: An interval's distance is the area above its own slice of the time axis, here 75 + 350 = 425 m.

options.text: The whole graph's area divided by eight
options.explanation: There is no rule tying an interval to a fixed fraction of the total; slice the base instead.

options.text: The velocity values at 70 s and 90 s
options.explanation: Two heights are not a distance; the area between them over the interval is.

options.text: The area of the largest single shape on the graph
options.explanation: The largest shape may sit anywhere on the timeline; interval questions slice, not cherry-pick.

questions.stem: A velocity-time line curves gently instead of staying straight. How is the distance still estimated?

options.text: Divide the curved region into many triangles and rectangles and add them
options.explanation: The same shape arithmetic, applied in small pieces, estimates the area under a curve.

options.text: Curved lines carry no area, so distance cannot be found
options.explanation: The area exists under any line; only the exact formulas need the straightness.

options.text: Read the final velocity and multiply by the total time
options.explanation: That rectangle uses only the endpoint and misses the shape of the whole profile.

options.text: Take the gradient of the curve and quote it
options.explanation: Gradient reads acceleration; the question asks for distance.

questions.stem: State how each enclosed section's area is interpreted when a journey is split into pieces.
questions.modelAnswer: Each enclosed section's area is the distance travelled during that section's own interval of time.

questions.stem: Recall the five areas of the worked car journey in order and their total.
questions.modelAnswer: The areas are 350 m, 525 m, 75 m, 350 m and 875 m, and their total distance is 2175 m.

questions.stem: Explain why labelling each enclosed area before calculating protects the final answer.
questions.modelAnswer: Labelling turns one long calculation into five short, checkable ones: if the total looks wrong, each labelled area can be tested against its own base and height. Without labels, a single slip is buried in the sum and cannot be traced, which is exactly where method marks are lost.

questions.stem: A delivery van's graph shows a triangle (base 30 s, height 10 m/s), then a rectangle (base 40 s, height 10 m/s), then a triangle back to rest (base 50 s). Calculate the total distance of the delivery run.
questions.modelAnswer: Triangle 1: ½ × 30 × 10 = 150 m. Rectangle: 40 × 10 = 400 m. Triangle 2: ½ × 50 × 10 = 250 m. Total distance = 150 + 400 + 250 = 800 m.
